why_angle: The cited pages give only yearly railing yields (solar.com) or California's 1,200 W plug-in cap (pluginsolartracker.com). None says that a south-facing panel hung vertically on a railing makes its least in June: NREL's PVWatts gives about 0.24 kWh a day for 200 W in Los Angeles. That June figure is why one panel is not enough and two panels in series is the right size for a 60 V / 10 A station like the AC180.

page.title: Balcony Solar Generator: How Many Railing Panels You Need (2026)
page.h1: Balcony solar generator: what railing panels actually make, month by month
page.desc: A balcony solar generator charges from panels on your railing. See month-by-month railing yields, series wiring for the BLUETTI AC180, and which kit fits your balcony.
page.answer: Short answer. A balcony solar generator is a battery charged by solar panels on the railing, and never feeds home wiring. Best for most: the BLUETTI AC180 with two 200 W panels in series, about 0.49 kWh a day in June (Los Angeles), the railing's worst month, versus 0.24 kWh for one panel.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Every yield figure comes from NREL's PVWatts model. The panel faces south and hangs vertically (90° tilt) in Los Angeles, with 14% system losses and no shade from the balcony above, so treat each figure as a ceiling.

  • Two panels double the worst month. In June, 400 W gives 14.64 kWh ÷ 30 days = 0.49 kWh a day, and 200 W gives 7.32 ÷ 30 = 0.24 kWh.
  • Winter is the railing's best season. Two panels give 45.50 kWh ÷ 31 = 1.47 kWh a day; one panel gives 22.75 ÷ 31 = 0.73.
  • June refill time. AC180 with two panels: 1,152 Wh ÷ 488 Wh a day = 2.4 days. With one panel: 1,152 ÷ 244 = 4.7 days. Charging losses and anything plugged in make both longer.
  • What a day's sun runs. Solar.com puts an ENERGY STAR fridge at about 460 kWh a year, or 460 ÷ 365 = 1.26 kWh a day. Two railing panels make 1.47 kWh a day in December, enough to cover it. In June they make 0.49 kWh, which covers 0.49 ÷ 1.26 = 39%.
  • Railing length. Each SP200L is 2,105 mm (82.8 in) long and 608 mm (23.9 in) tall unfolded, so two side by side need 2 × 2,105 = 4.21 m (13.8 ft).
  • Bundle saving. The AC180 ($499) and the 2-panel pack ($798) cost $1,297 bought separately; the bundle is $1,232, which saves $65.
Your balconyWhat fits
South railing 4.2 m (13.8 ft) or longer, and you want useful charging in summerAC180 + 2 × 200 W, wired in series
About 2.1 m (6.9 ft) of railing, used mainly for winter or outage backupAC180 + 1 × 200 W
The panels can lie on a stand at about 30° instead of hangingTilt them: in New York a tilted 200 W panel gives 26.32 kWh in June against 8.82 kWh hanging
The station would have to sit outsideKeep it indoors: the AC180 charges only from 0 to 40 °C (32–104 °F), so run the 5 m cable through the door

{kit:kit-ac180-two-panels-series} Pick this if your railing is long enough for two panels. It is the only one of these sets that still makes about half a kilowatt-hour a day in June. Together the two panels deliver 400 W, inside the AC180's 500 W solar limit. BLUETTI's listing images show the SP200L as the bundle's panel.

{kit:kit-ac180-one-panel} Pick this if you have room for one panel or mostly want the battery for outages. It makes 0.73 kWh a day in December and 0.24 kWh in June, and you can add a second SP200L in series later. BLUETTI's FAQ says mixing panel models is "not encouraged", so add the same model.

The Elite 100 V2 + 200W bundle costs less ($729) and takes up to 20 A and 1,000 W of solar. But its in-box list has an AC cable, the manual and a grounding screw, with no solar cable. BLUETTI sells a 20 A MC4-to-XT60 cable that lists the Elite 100 V2 as compatible ($29 on 2026-11-13), so add it to the order.

Why a railing panel is a winter panel

A panel hung on a railing stands vertical. Low winter sun hits it almost face-on, while high June sun strikes it at a steep angle. Output therefore peaks in winter and bottoms out in summer, the reverse of a tilted rooftop panel.

PVWatts, south-facingJuneWinter monthYear
400 W on a railing, Los Angeles14.64 kWh48.80 kWh (Nov), 45.50 kWh (Dec)404 kWh
200 W on a railing, New York8.82 kWh19.00 kWh (Jan)169 kWh
200 W tilted 30°, New York26.32 kWh14.30 kWh (Dec)264 kWh

How you wire the second panel decides whether its power reaches the battery. The AC180 accepts 12–60 V at up to 10 A and 500 W. Each SP200L is rated 24.6 V open-circuit and 10.8 A short-circuit.

  • Series (panel 1's + to panel 2's −): 2 × 24.6 = 49.2 V, and the current stays at 10.8 A, so the full 400 W can reach the station. The two free leads go into one extension cable, then into the AC180's own 1.5 m solar charging cable.
  • Parallel (MC4 Y-branch): 2 × 10.8 = 21.6 A against a 10 A cap, which allows at most 24.6 V × 10 A = 246 W, and less in practice.

Turn the AC outlets off when nothing needs them. The Solar Lab calculated the Elite 100 V2's idle draw at about 16 W with the AC inverter on and no load. Over a day that is 16 W × 24 h = 384 Wh, more than one 200 W railing panel's 244 Wh a day in a Los Angeles June.

Not recommended

The 3 × 200 W panel pack for an AC180. BLUETTI sells the SP200L as a 3-pack ($1,197). Three in series reach 3 × 24.6 = 73.8 V, over the AC180's 60 V limit. The manual says panels above 60 V open-circuit voltage will damage the unit, and it reports PV over-voltage as error E033. Three in parallel run into the same 10 A cap as two. For the AC180, stop at two panels in series.
